q: Which statement correctly distinguishes abstraction from encapsulation?

q: What is the difference between opening a file with ios::app and opening it with ios::ate?

opts.C: ios::app opens the file for reading only, whereas ios::ate opens it for writing only

q: Why is an exception of class type normally caught by reference rather than by value?

opts.A: Catching a class type by value is rejected by the compiler
opts.B: A by-value handler copies the thrown object and slices a derived exception down to the handler's base type
opts.C: Only a by-reference handler permits the exception to be rethrown to an outer try block
opts.D: A by-value handler suppresses the unwinding of objects created inside the try block

q: A try block lists a handler for catch (const std::exception&) before a handler for catch (const std::out_of_range&). What happens when an out_of_range object is thrown inside that try block?

opts.A: The out_of_range handler runs, because it is the more derived and therefore the better match
opts.B: Both handlers run, the base one first and the derived one afterwards
opts.C: The std::exception handler runs, because handlers are examined in the order they are written
opts.D: The program calls std::terminate, because this ordering of handlers is ill-formed

q: For a std::string holding 5 characters, how does at(9) differ in behaviour from operator[](9)?

opts.B: Both silently return a reference to the string's terminating null character
opts.C: at(9) returns a default-constructed char, while operator[](9) throws std::length_error
opts.D: at(9) throws std::out_of_range, while operator[](9) is unchecked and gives undefined behaviour
